583.title: discussion — settling what an agent cannot read off disk
583.content: Skill discussion: Settle which harness, and which repositories, when no file says: the output is a document conforming to discussion.output.schema.json. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . An agent that has just read bootstrap’s README.md knows the shape of a harness and nothing about this one. Two questions have no answer in any file it can reach: . | which harness this repository should become: bootstrap itself, or any Harness built on it; | which repositories are involved — where the dependency is read from, where the new declaration is written to, and whether they are the same. | . Only whoever asked for the harness can answer them, so the agent asks. This skill says what the asking must produce. processes/discussion.bpmn narrows the candidates and then calls human-agent-discussion, the one reusable way bootstrap asks a person anything, with no default allowed.

584.title: Inputs and outputs
584.content: |   |   | . | in | discussion.input.schema.json: what the agent already knows, and which of the two unknowns is open | . | out | discussion.output.schema.json: harness, repositories[], outcome, determinedBy, answeredBy, and the exchange that produced it | . Both are plain JSON Schema in schemas/, readable with nothing installed. The task is finished when a document conforming to the output schema exists, not when a conversation has taken place. The participant may be a person or a sibling agent that already holds the answer; the output records which (kind: person | agent), as human-agent-discussion says.

585.title: First, say where you are
585.content: Before narrowing anything (A_DetermineWhere), determine the three things human-agent-discussion requires before any question: . | the Process: Initialize a harness, inside Determine the harness and repositories. A Bootstrapping Agent can be nowhere else (FR-2); | the Roles: itself as the Bootstrapping Agent; the person it will ask as the Requestor. A request relayed by somebody else leaves the Requestor undetermined; | the context: what the request said, and what the checkout holds. | . One that cannot be determined is never filled with a default: it is asked about first, and the harness question waits.

586.title: Rules
586.content: Ask the fewest questions that settle it. Narrow the candidate list from context first (a repository whose root already holds a declaration, <name>.json, is not a blank slate) and put the rest as one question with the candidates named. A question a reader must go and research is not ready. Never infer the answer from a default. If nothing is known, the output’s determinedBy is asked, not assumed. assumed is permitted only for a default the README states, and assumption then names it. Record repositories as pairs, not as a list. read from and written to can be the same repository or two; the point of determining them is to know where the declaration lands. Never infer written-to from push access. A remote repository is read-from until the Requestor authorizes writing to it (confirm-harness). A refusal is an outcome. If the participant declines, that is outcome: "unsettled" with what was asked and what is still open — not a guess, and not an error.

594.title: /dispatch-agent — parallel dispatch with a live 2-minute status heartbeat
594.content: Skill dispatch-agent: Dispatch one or more background sub-agents against parallel research/build fronts with a STANDARDIZED live progress contract, and monitor them on a 2-minute heartbeat. Every dispatched agent emits consistent DID/DOING/NEXT/BLOCKERS blocks with real log output (not static “still running”); the parent extracts the latest block from each agent every ~120 s and posts one consolidated synthesis table. Use when the user says “dispatch agents”, “fan out”, “run these in parallel with monitoring”, “give me status every 2 minutes”, or when you are about to launch ≥ 2 background Agents on independent work. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . The expensive failure mode of multi-agent dispatch is going dark: you launch N background agents, then can’t say what any of them is doing until it completes 20 minutes later. This skill fixes that with two halves that MUST be used together: . | Agent-side progress contract — every dispatched agent emits a consistent, machine-greppable progress block on a fixed cadence, with live evidence (log tails, exit codes, counts), never a static “still working on it”. | Parent-side 2-minute heartbeat — the parent extracts the latest block from each running agent every ~120 s and posts ONE consolidated synthesis table to the user, so monitoring is passive and effortless. | . Both halves are load-bearing. An agent that doesn’t follow the contract can’t be synthesized; a parent that doesn’t run the heartbeat leaves the user blind. Do not dispatch without both.

595.title: 0a. Interactive child session vs background agent — choose FIRST (owner directive 2026-11-25, STRICT)
595.content: Owner, verbatim: “If you are swarming a process around research that might require interaction with the author or owner then that should be a proper child sibling that is interactive not a spawning process that you can’t engage in. … This should be a general practice unless it’s known that the swarm activities very mechanical and does not need any human attraction.” . A background Agent (this skill’s default) cannot be steered: the owner cannot see it, talk to it, or answer its questions. So before dispatching, classify each front: . | front | how to launch | . | Research / derivation / open question — a route choice, a modelling or convention choice, a definition the corpus leaves open, anything whose next step may need the owner | Interactive child session: mcp__claude-code-remote__create_session (with source_url of the repo and a self-contained prompt). It appears in the owner’s session list; the owner can read and steer it, and it asks the owner directly (AskUserQuestion, chat-mirrored). Tell it to send progress to the parent with send_message. | . | Mechanical — a known procedure with one right answer: re-run a producer, attribute a measured change, refresh witnesses, apply a ruled fix, a lint/audit drain | Background Agent is fine. Any owner decision it surfaces is framed in its report and relayed by the parent. | . | Unsure | Treat as research → interactive child session. | . Rules for an interactive research child: . | Its prompt must say it is interactive, must ask the owner at forks rather than guess, and must post its pre-registered plan to the owner before computing. | It inherits every repository discipline (anti-fit, NO-FLOAT64, Strict Lean, no lake build, fences); put the essentials in the prompt, because it starts with no context. | The parent records the child’s session id on the bean and in its progress report, so the owner can find it. | If a background agent turns out to need owner input, stop it, check its worktree for unpushed work, and relaunch the front as an interactive child session with that context. | .

596.title: 0. When to use
596.content: . | Launching ≥ 2 background Agent calls on independent fronts (research routes, per-file proofs, per-isotope compute). | The user asks for periodic status (“update me every 2 minutes”, “keep me posted”, “monitor these”). | A single long agent whose progress the user wants to watch live. | . For a single quick synchronous agent whose result you need before the next step, skip this — just call Agent(run_in_background: false).

597.title: 1. Agent-side progress contract (PASTE THIS into every dispatched agent)
597.content: Append the block below verbatim to every agent prompt you dispatch through this skill. Fill in <LABEL> with a short stable tag (≤ 16 chars, kebab-case: a3-offblock, ctil-root, a4-interface) — the parent keys the synthesis table on it. ## PROGRESS REPORTING CONTRACT (STRICT — the parent monitors you on this) Your label is: <LABEL> Emit a progress block **as a plain-text assistant message** (not a tool call) at EVERY meaningful step, and **at least once every ~90 seconds of wall time** even mid-step. Use this EXACT shape so the parent can grep and synthesize it: ### ⟦PROGRESS⟧ <LABEL> · step N DID: <what you just finished — CONCRETE evidence only: file paths, lean exit codes, real-sorry counts, git shas, row counts, the tail of a log. NOT "worked on the proof".> DOING: <the step in flight right now. If a command is RUNNING, quote the last 3–8 relevant lines of its output / the key live metric (elapsed, % done, current goal state, error so far). NEVER a canned "still running" — show the live log.> NEXT: <the single concrete next action you will take.> BLOCKERS: <none | the precise blocker (missing lemma name, 403, ENOSPC, evicted oleans, ambiguous spec).> Rules that keep updates LIVE, not semi-static: - **Tee every long command to a log and quote its tail** in DOING: `<cmd> 2>&1 | tee /tmp/<LABEL>-<step>.log` then put the last lines in the block. A Lean check, a python compute, a git op > ~10 s all qualify. - **Advance the step counter** every block; never repeat an identical block twice — if nothing changed, say what you are still waiting on and quote the newest log line. - **Evidence or it didn't happen**: every DID line names a file / exit code / count / sha. No vague verbs. - When you finish, emit a final block with marker `### ⟦DONE⟧ <LABEL>` carrying the verdict (closed / scope-(a) / scope-(b) / bean-the-gap), the exact .lean path(s), lean-direct exit code, real-sorry count, and the branch you pushed. Why this exact shape: the parent’s extractor (below) greps for the ⟦PROGRESS⟧ / ⟦DONE⟧ markers and pulls the DID/DOING/NEXT/BLOCKERS lines. Consistent markers → one-line-per-agent synthesis with zero guessing. Deviating from the marker or the four keys breaks the monitor. This contract is additive to the task’s own discipline (anti-fit, lean-direct verification, zero-sorry, bean-the-gap). It governs how the agent reports, never what counts as done. An agent still may not launder a fit or fake a closure to make its DID line look better — honesty over a pretty status.

598.title: 2. Dispatch procedure
598.content: . | Scope each front to one independent agent (no shared files between agents — worktree isolation makes parallel file writes safe; use isolation: "worktree" whenever agents mutate the tree). | Assign each a <LABEL> and paste both: . | the §1 progress contract block above, AND | the Mandatory Sibling Launch Briefing from swarm-sibling-launch.md (Template A for the single merge-steward, Template B for every Coding / Proof / Prose / Compute Sibling — injecting .claude/skills/local/*.md, continual-progress.md, idle-backlog.md, merge-queue.md sibling-side submission with zero self-merging, one-voice external-reader hygiene, two-step witness SHA stamping, reverting the 9 qou-v0t8 contended audit witnesses, CPU throttling, and branch/public-release fences). | . | Launch all agents in a single message (multiple Agent tool calls) so they run concurrently. Record each returned agentId ↔ <LABEL> mapping in a scratch note (/tmp/<session>-dispatch-map.txt) so the heartbeat can label rows even before an agent’s first block lands. | Immediately arm the heartbeat (§3). Do not end the turn without it. | .

599.title: 3. Parent-side 2-minute heartbeat
599.content: 3a. The extractor (targeted — never read the full JSONL) . Reading an agent’s whole *.output transcript overflows context. Extract ONLY the latest progress block per agent. Save this once as scripts/agent-progress.py (or inline it): . #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Usage: agent-progress.py <tasks-dir> # Prints the latest ⟦PROGRESS⟧/⟦DONE⟧ block from each agent's *.output JSONL. import json, re, sys, glob, os tasks = sys.argv[1] for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(tasks, "*.output"))): aid = os.path.basename(f)[:-7] last = None try: for line in open(f): try: o = json.loads(line) except Exception: continue for c in (o.get("message", {}).get("content") or []): if isinstance(c, dict) and c.get("type") == "text": t = c.get("text", "") if "⟦PROGRESS⟧" in t or "⟦DONE⟧" in t: # keep only from the last marker onward idx = max(t.rfind("⟦PROGRESS⟧"), t.rfind("⟦DONE⟧")) last = t[t.rfind("###", 0, idx):] if idx >= 0 else t except FileNotFoundError: continue done = last and "⟦DONE⟧" in last print(f"===== {aid[:12]} {'[DONE]' if done else '[live]'} =====") print((last or "(no progress block yet — agent still spinning up)").strip()[:900]) print() . Run it against the session tasks dir: python3 scripts/agent-progress.py "$TASKS_DIR" where $TASKS_DIR is the tasks/ folder holding the <agentId>.output files (the dispatch tool result names each output_file; its parent dir is $TASKS_DIR). 🛑 That dir also holds the stdout of every BACKGROUNDED BASH JOB, and a glob cannot tell them apart by name. Measured 2026-10-10: a heartbeat over a dir with one agent and six backgrounded Bash commands printed seven rows, six reading [live] (no progress block yet — agent still spinning up) — for a pip install, a setup-folio-assistant.sh and a precision-gates.sh run. They never advance, because a Bash job emits no ⟦PROGRESS⟧ block, so they read as permanently-hung agents and invite a SendMessage nudge to something that cannot receive one. And it buried a real signal: one of the six had TIMED OUT (GATE_EXIT=124) while its row said “spinning up”. scripts/agent-progress.py now discriminates on the first line — an agent transcript is JSONL whose first record carries isSidechain/parentUuid/promptId; Bash stdout is arbitrary text — and announces the count it skipped rather than filtering silently. Same dir, after the fix: (skipped 7 non-agent .output file(s)) then one row. Two consequences for the heartbeat. A [live] row with no block is only evidence about an agent if the file is an agent transcript — check before nudging. And cat the Bash job’s own .output when you want its result; the extractor deliberately will not show it, and a 0-byte file under a | tail pipeline means “not finished”, not “crashed”. 3b. The cadence . Every ~120 s while any agent is still [live]: . | Run the extractor. | Post ONE consolidated synthesis to the user — a compact table, one row per agent, newest block only: . | label | DID (evidence) | DOING (live) | NEXT | BLOCKERS |——-|—————-|————–|——|———-| . Keep it to one screen. If a block is stale (same step counter as last heartbeat and > 3 min old), flag it ⚠ stale and note you’ll SendMessage the agent to nudge it. | Re-arm the next 120 s tick, then end the turn (do not busy-wait). | . Cadence mechanism — do NOT foreground-sleep (blocked). Use one of: . | ScheduleWakeup with delaySeconds: 120, prompt: "/dispatch-agent heartbeat", reason: "2-min agent status heartbeat" — the standard dynamic-loop tick. Call ScheduleWakeup({stop:true}) once every agent is [DONE]. | If the harness surfaces agent-completion notifications, those also wake you; run the extractor on each and treat it as an off-cadence heartbeat, then re-arm the 120 s fallback so quiet stretches still tick. | . The 120 s tick is a fallback heartbeat, not the only signal — completion notifications arrive on their own. Pick 120 s because the user asked for 2-minute updates; honor that literally. 3c. Nudging a silent agent . If an agent shows (no progress block yet) for > 3 min, or its step counter hasn’t advanced across two heartbeats, `SendMessage(to: . , ...)` with a one-line nudge: *"Emit a fresh ⟦PROGRESS⟧ block with the live tail of whatever is running."* An agent that has genuinely hung (evicted oleans, ENOSPC) will surface it as a BLOCKER once nudged. --- ## 4. On completion When an agent emits `⟦DONE⟧` (or the harness notifies completion): 1. Drop it from the `[live]` set; keep its final block in the synthesis as a `[DONE]` row. 2. **Verify before trusting the DONE line.** The agent's self-reported "sorry-free / exit 0" is a claim — the parent re-runs lean-direct on each edited `.lean` itself (exit 0, no `declaration uses 'sorry'`) before merging, exactly as for any dispatched Lean work. A green DID line never substitutes for the parent's own verification. 3. When **all** agents are `[DONE]`: post a final consolidated synthesis (verdict per front + the merge/next-step queue), `ScheduleWakeup( {stop:true})`, and end the heartbeat. --- ## 5. Anti-patterns (each is a skill violation) - **Going dark** — dispatching background agents without arming the heartbeat. The user then has to ask "what's happening?" — the exact friction this skill removes. - **Semi-static updates** — "agent still running the proof" with no log tail, no step counter, no evidence. If a command is in flight, the block MUST carry its live output. - **Reading the full transcript** — tailing/`cat`-ing the `*.output` JSONL into context instead of using the targeted extractor. Overflows context and defeats the point. - **Trusting the DONE line** — merging on an agent's self-reported "exit 0" without the parent's own lean-direct re-verification. - **Wrong cadence** — 5-minute or "when I remember" ticks when the user asked for 2 minutes. Honor the literal cadence.

602.title: Inputs and outputs
602.content: schemas/skills/dmn-authoring/: . | in — decisionName (required), inputVariables (required), sourceLogic | out — dmnFile, decisionTableCount, ruleCount, hitPolicy | .

603.title: A computed gateway is not a chosen one
603.content: In this repository a DMN table has a second job: an exclusive gateway carrying <cat-harness.processes:decision ref="decisions/<file>.dmn#<Decision_Id>"/> has its branch computed from the table rather than picked by the agent. workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at such a gateway. Asserting the answer would defeat the point of writing the table. You pass facts — e.g. { failCritical: 0, failMajor: 2 } from qa_sweep totals — and the table returns the branch. Adding one means adding the .dmn, the cat-harness.processes:decision ref, and nothing else: the loader checks that every outcome the table can return names a real outgoing flow, so a table that can route somewhere the diagram cannot go is a load error rather than a surprise at the moment of decision.

604.title: The FEEL subset this interpreter implements
604.content: src/workflow/decision-table.ts implements a deliberate subset: - (any), literals, comparisons, and one-of. It refuses ranges, not() and function calls rather than mis-evaluating them. Write within that subset: a table using a construct the interpreter rejects fails at load, rather than being mis-evaluated at the moment of decision.

605.title: Three states belong in the table
605.content: Encode “could not determine” as an outcome in its own right — pages-live-gate.dmn returns live, not-yet and unknown; folio-intent.dmn returns ask when the filesystem cannot decide. A gate whose only outcomes are pass and fail forces an unmeasured input to be rendered as one of them, and it is always rendered as pass. If your decision has an input that may be unavailable, give it a branch.

606.title: Hit policy
606.content: Say it explicitly. FIRST is the usual choice here and is what folio-intent.dmn uses — rules are ordered, the first match wins, and the ordering is then part of the logic and must be reviewed as such.

607.title: When a layer above transforms it
607.content: A layer built on this one may render decision tables for human review or derive other artefacts (questionnaires, for instance) from them. Then the DMN is a source artefact, not documentation of one; that layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics and the caveats, and this one names no layer above it.

610.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
610.title: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
610.content: Process_Ingestion · advisory · 4 step(s) . Accepts an upload, records its extracted metadata in the knowledge graph, and catalogues the asset in library/ — held if materialized, referenced if not. THE BASIC FLOW, with very little process context assumed. Accept, extract the metadata into the KG, ask whether the asset is materialized, place it in library/<slug>/. It calls NO subprocess and makes no content-type decision. THE ID Process_Ingestion IS KEPT ON PURPOSE: methodology-from-source.bpmn’s Call_Ingest names it, and so does every higher-layer process that refines this flow. Refinement is by INVERSION — a refining process calls this one as its first step and continues with its own work; nothing here names a refinement, because the corpus has no BPMN extension point and a harness diagram naming a higher one would be an upward edge. The document pipeline (rungs, the four ingest phases, the L1 completeness gate, promotion, the summary queue) is such a refinement, in the layer above. i i i i Actors: Contributor (human or agent) · Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) .

611.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/

612.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
612.title: Lanes — who acts
612.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Contributor (human or agent) | user | Whoever puts the file in the queue.“HUMAN OR AGENT” IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT A HEDGE: both place files here. That is why Task_Place is a plain bpmn:task rather than a userTask — asserting a human performs it would contradict the lane’s own role graph, which is what activity-fulfilment-kind exists to catch.WHAT THE LANE IS ACCOUNTABLE FOR, and where it ends. Choosing a route, writing the bytes into the DECLARED queue of the layer that will own them, and discharging afterwards whatever that route could not — the web form has no working tree, so no pre-commit hook and no generator runs on it. The lane does NOT ingest and does not clean the queue: it hands over, and Lane_1 takes it from there. upload-routes carries the routes and their obligations. | . | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | ingestion-agent | Runs the basic flow from the metadata step to the placement in library/, unattended: every decision in it is decidable from the material and its declarations. It asks one question — is the asset materialized? — and that is answered from the materialization state vocabulary (schemas/kg/materialization-state.ts), not by judgement. It does NOT choose a reader for the bytes, derive sections or blocks, or describe images: those are a refining process’s work, which calls this flow first.THE FLOW ENDS IN THIS LANE. The asset catalogued in library/ — held, or recorded as referenced — is the terminal state, and every knowledge-graph reference to it resolves through library/ from here; a refining process continues from it rather than being drawn into this one. There is no separate corpus lane: it would hold only the end event, and a lane with no activity has no performer to describe. | .

613.doc: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/
613.title: Steps
613.content: Every one of the 4 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Place it in uploads/ by a declared routeTask_Place | Contributor (human or agent) | upload-routes | THE FIRST LINK: everything downstream of here takes a file that is already in the queue, so without this step how the file got there is governed by nothing.WHAT THIS STEP IS. The basic flow’s ACCEPT step: choosing an arrival route, writing the bytes into the declared queue of the layer that will own them, and discharging what that route does not discharge for you. The routes, what each writer owes, and the two that are mechanisms against the one that is a persona are in the upload-routes skill; upload-url composes the forge URL for the web route from the declaration rather than from a literal, because a hand-written one can 404.WHY A PLAIN bpmn:task AND NOT A userTask. A userTask asserts a human performs it, and this lane is “Contributor (human or agent)” because both do; asserting human-only would be an activity-fulfilment-kind contradiction. A plain task asserts nothing about the performer.WHY THE BEAN OP IS note AND NOT claim. Placing a file claims nothing; it adds to a queue. What it owes the work plan is visibility. A note against the ingestion bean is what makes the queue’s growth something another session can see. | . | Extract its metadata into the KGTask_ExtractMetadata | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | asset-extraction | THE METADATA STEP. What enters the knowledge graph is the asset’s INDEX — what it is, how big, what type, when it says it was written — and, for a container, what is in it; its contents do not go in unless somebody asks, with a reason. The tool is cat-harness-tools/scripts/extract-assets.ts, writing a folio-extraction/v1 record (schemas/content/extraction.ts).The media type is sniffed from the leading bytes, never taken from the extension. | . | **Place the asset in library//**`Task_PlaceInLibrary` | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | library-ingestion | The materialized branch. The asset lands in library/<slug>/ with its metadata record, its provenance and its fixity. The folder name IS the citation key, so a citation and a directory are the same string.The upload is then RETIRED, not left and not deleted: it moves to fsh-guts/uploads/ beside a sidecar naming where it came from and when, and check:uploads-retired finds one that was not. A refining process that derives content from the bytes does so before that retirement; library-ingestion carries the rule. | . | Record it in library/ as referencedTask_CatalogueReference | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | library-ingestion | The referenced branch. Nothing is fetched and no bytes are written: the catalogue record says where the asset is and that we hold none. A reference is not a fetch — it stays navigable without being held, and materializing it later is materialize-remote.bpmn’s decision, with its purpose and five gates, not this flow’s. | .

Collapsing referenced into materialized is the failure the vocabulary exists to stop: corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a referenced node placed as held reads as present to every consumer. | materialized → Place the asset in library//**referenced** → Record it in library/ as referenced | .

616.title: Document Intake
616.content: Skill document-intake: Process uploaded documents (PDFs, scans, LaTeX, WHO L1/L2 guidelines, etc.) from library/ into structured content objects. Handles OCR extraction, environment detection, structural analysis, and content-object generation. Supports multi-stage pipelines: raw upload → extracted text → structured blocks → .ts/.md content objects. Named by: Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Bib human-review integration (2026-06-09). Track per-upload ingestion status in library/intake.json (identified passage, formalised?, matched?) and link each upload to the references.ts entry it sources. An upload that supplies a cited source moves that ref to source-in-repo (agent-identified passage; no human photo) and then through the local/bib-human-review ladder to validated. Existing library/ follow the same agent-sourced path (design §5). Per-upload state now lives in the source ledger (2026-08-08). The library/<id>/intake.json convention below covers 1 of the corpus’s 284 documents; the per-document row — reference join, examination status, and relevance verdict — is now the source ledger (source-ledger/v1, now test/attestations/bib-verification/), populated by local/paper-relevance-triage. Use the ledger for “what is this document, is it cited, does it matter”; keep intake.json for the multi-stage extraction state of a document actually being converted (OCR → blocks → content objects). Do not record a title, author, or year in the ledger — bibliographic metadata belongs in folio/schema/references.ts alone.

617.title: Overview
617.content: This skill manages the library/ directory as an intake pipeline for converting raw documents into structured content objects. It handles: . | Scanned PDFs / images — OCR extraction → text → blocks | LaTeX source — environment extraction → blocks | WHO L1 → L2 guidelines — normative structure → blocks | arXiv papers — fetched source → blocks (delegates to paper-importer) | Arbitrary documents — best-effort structural analysis | . The key distinction from paper-importer: this skill owns the full lifecycle of library/, including tracking processing state, partial extractions, and multi-pass refinement. Paper-importer focuses on the final content-object generation step.

618.title: When to Use This Skill
618.content: . | User says “upload”, “scan”, “process document”, “intake” | User drops a file into library/ | User mentions WHO, L1, L2, guideline, normative | User wants to convert a raw document into content objects | Files appear in library/ that haven’t been processed yet | .

619.title: library/ Directory Convention
619.content: library/ <document-id>/ intake.json ← processing state + metadata original.pdf ← raw upload (PDF, scan, etc.) original.tex ← or LaTeX source extracted-text.md ← OCR or parser output (intermediate) extracted-blocks.json ← structured extraction (intermediate) mapping.json ← label/section mapping decisions README.md ← human notes about the document . intake.json schema . { "id": "who-anc-2016", "title": "WHO Recommendations on Antenatal Care", "source": { "type": "pdf", "url": "https://...", "fetchedAt": "2026-03-25T..." }, "format": "pdf|latex|scan|html|docx", "pipeline": { "stage": "uploaded|extracted|structured|mapped|generated", "extractedAt": null, "structuredAt": null, "generatedAt": null, "errors": [] }, "classification": { "type": "guideline|paper|report|standard", "domain": "health|physics|math|...", "normativeLevel": "L1|L2|L3|null" }, "chapters": [], "blockCount": 0, "targetPaper": "content/<paper-id>/" } .

620.title: Pipeline Stages
620.content: Stage 1: Upload (→ uploaded) . Place raw files in library/<document-id>/. Create intake.json with source metadata. Files are committed to git for reproducibility. Supported formats: . | PDF — academic papers, scanned guidelines, reports | LaTeX — .tex source bundles | HTML — web-published guidelines, standards | DOCX — Word documents (WHO often distributes as Word) | Images — scanned pages (PNG, JPG, TIFF) | . For academic papers, prefer the MCP fetch path (added 2026-05-22): when the session network allows the upstream host, use paper-search-mcp (arxiv / PubMed / bioRxiv / medRxiv) or openalex-paper-search (alex-mcp; OpenAlex catalog) rather than curl/WebFetch. The MCP tools return canonical metadata and the PDF in one call, eliminating the OCR-then-extract-then-name dance. See paper-importer.md §Phase 1 for the per-tool routing table. Sandboxed Claude-Code-on-the-web sessions (github-only allowlist) cannot reach those hosts; in those sessions, queue the fetch onto a normal-network machine per bib-qa.md §Batch intake pipeline. Stage 2: Extraction (→ extracted) . Convert raw format to extracted-text.md: . 🛑 THIS SECTION WAS 82 LINES BEHIND ITS SOURCE UNTIL 2026-09-16, and the stale version named tools instead of programs. It said “PDF (text) | pdftotext or PDF.js” and “PDF (scan) | Tesseract OCR / Claude vision” — which is precisely the aspirational text scripts/pdf-extract.py was written to replace. That script’s own docstring records the cost: “document-intake advertises ‘Handles OCR extraction’ and its routing table sends scanned PDFs to ‘Tesseract OCR / Claude vision’ — but nothing implemented that, so in practice an agent reached for a Python PDF library, got an empty string or an import crash, and had to guess what went wrong.” . The folio-assistant copy was fixed then; this one was not, and qou is where all 715 ingested documents live. The drift gate (gen-skill-docs.ts --check) covers the published docs site only — nothing checks this file against its source, so assume it can go stale again and diff it against skills/folio-paper-adapter/document-intake.md before trusting it. The scripts live in the folio-assistant clone, not in qou. Invoke them across the boundary, as scripts/migrate-uploads-to-library.py already does: . | Format | Extraction method | . | PDF (text) | folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-extract.py — a 5-rung ladder, not one tool | . | PDF (scan) | pdf-extract.py exits 2, then folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-ocr.py (Tesseract) or Claude vision | . | PDF (sections) | folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-structure.py → structure.json + sections/*.md | . | PDF (tables/figures) | folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-tables.py → tables.json, multipage stitching included | . | LaTeX | Direct parse (strip preamble) | . | HTML | Readability + turndown | . | DOCX | Pandoc → markdown | . | Images | Claude vision API | . python3 folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-extract.py FILE.pdf -o extracted-text.md python3 folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-ocr.py FILE.pdf --outdir library/<doc-id>/ # scans only python3 folio-assistant/scripts/pdf-structure.py FILE.pdf --outdir library --ocr python3 folio-assistant/scripts/extract-candidates.py library/<doc-id>/ . Four things that matter here and are not guessable from the table: . | The exit code is the diagnosis. pdf-extract.py returns 0 text · 2 no text layer, i.e. a scan · 3 a parser problem on a file that does have text · 4 bad usage. So “swap libraries” and “you need OCR” are decided by evidence rather than by trying things. | pdf-structure.py READS the OCR cache; it never runs OCR. 626.title: Evidence Appraisal
626.content: Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Board: place a note . Appraise and grade a body of evidence against the grading system the folio declares. This skill supplies the procedure; it does not supply the system.

627.title: Why this skill names no grading system
627.content: Which grading system applies is a methodological commitment of the folio and the body that publishes it; the platform holds no subject matter, and a hardcoded system would leave every folio that uses another one working around the platform. An evidence-retrieval process in the content layer judges certainty “per the grading system the folio declares”. This skill covers what appraisal is, what it attaches to, and what has to survive as a record afterwards. Domain layers supply concrete grading systems as refinement skills and code lists (certainty levels, rating reasons, recommendation strength). Each applies only when declared, never as a default; with nothing declared, appraisal is refused.

628.title: Responsibilities
628.content: . | Appraise the body of evidence assembled for one question, not a citation | Record the grade with its reasons, not as a bare label | Distinguish “the evidence is weak” from “there is not enough to judge” | Re-appraise when the body changes, and say what moved the grade | Refuse to grade when no system is declared, rather than picking one | .

629.title: The unit is the body, not the citation
629.content: The grade attaches to the body of evidence for one PICO question. This is why appraisal sits after retrieval’s parallel join and not inside the fan-out: the three retrieval classes (trusted L1 sources, trusted L2/L3 content, data repositories) contribute to one judgement; grading each branch separately would produce three numbers that answer no question. A single citation does not carry a certainty grade.

630.title: “Cannot appraise” is a third state
630.content: Three outcomes; “not appraisable” is not a low grade: . | outcome | means | . | graded | the body was appraised and carries a certainty | . | not appraisable | too little retrieved, or no declared system, or the question was not framed as PICO | . | gap recorded | nothing authoritative was found, and that is the finding | . Never collapse “not appraisable” into the lowest grade: “we looked and the evidence is poor” is not “we could not look”. A recommendation resting on the first is weak; one resting on the second is unsupported.

631.title: Inputs
631.content: . | The framed PICO question — without it the search is not reproducible and the appraisal is not checkable | Candidates that passed an authority check, so authority is a resolved fact rather than an assertion in the citation | The grading system declared by the folio | .

632.title: Outputs
632.content: . | A certainty judgement for the body, in the declared system’s own vocabulary | The reasons, in enough detail that a later reader can tell whether they would still hold (decision-audit); a grade without them cannot be reviewed, only re-litigated | Any gap, recorded as a gap rather than as a low grade | .

633.title: This has nothing to do with formal content
633.content: A graded body of empirical evidence is never an input to a formal deductive proof. In a content type with a formal proof layer, a formal claim’s assertion is discharged by its machine-checked proof sibling and by nothing else; certainty grading belongs to empirical guidance about the world, where the question is what the evidence supports. An empirical grade in a formal proof obligation is a category error.

634.title: Actors
634.content: . | Author / guideline developer (lead) | Domain SME (domain judgement, supplied by the content-type layer) | Content Reviewer (checks the grade’s reasons survive, not the grade itself) | .

636.title: Evidence review — the same rule, a second instance
636.content: Skill evidence-review: Evidence review as an instance of untainted verification — the separation of the appraising party from the drafting party, what recurring surveillance in a living guideline shares with a stale QA verdict, and which of guideline methodology’s rules are fenced rather than shipped. Named by: Contributor feedback on a working draft . Skill id: evidence-review · Package: folio-core . untainted-verification states a generic discipline. Evidence review — the appraisal of the evidence behind a recommendation — is one instance of it; the translation round trip is another. Two unrelated instances are evidence that the discipline is generic, where one would only be an example.

637.title: The rule
637.content: The party that drafted the recommendation does not write the evidence appraisal for it. Guideline methodology already separates the systematic review team from the guideline development group for the same reason: a party assessing its own output is comparing a thing with its own paraphrase of itself. | untainted-verification | here | . | producer | whoever drafts the recommendation | . | checker — given the artefact, and nothing that would let it shortcut | the appraisal, given the question and the evidence, not the draft’s conclusion | . | adjudicator — given the intent and the checker’s output, never the artefact | the evidence-to-decision judgement | . An appraiser shown the drafted recommendation is told the answer before being asked the question; its “the evidence supports it” measures the instruction, not the literature.

638.title: Recurring surveillance is staleness, generalised
638.content: A living guideline is updated as evidence appears, so its appraisal is a verdict with an expiry. A QA verdict is hashed to its subject and stales when the subject is edited; a living-guideline verdict stales when the evidence base changes, even though the subject did not. The field_hash covers only inputs in the repository; an external corpus is not covered. Either way, “verified on DATE against THESE inputs” is a different claim from “verified”, because a reader given the second cannot tell a current verdict from a lapsed one. A folio implementing surveillance gives each verdict an explicit expiry, as bean-blocking (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) does for a block: a verdict with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one.

639.title: The fencing analysis — which rules are the platform’s, and which are not
639.content: Run through domain-fencing (opt-in cat-harness.kg-ops)’s three questions, in order, first-to-answer wins: . | candidate rule | Q1 rationale survives translation? | Q2 domain in mechanism or vocabulary? | Q3 needs the domain installed? | verdict | . | appraiser ≠ drafter | yes, word for word | vocabulary | no | platform — it IS the spine | . | a verdict carries what it was verified against, and when | yes — it is the field_hash argument | vocabulary | no | platform | . | a finding is upheld by opening the cited source, never by trusting the rule’s wording | yes | vocabulary | no | platform — and already the practice in voice-who-guideline-development | . | certainty rated across the GRADE domains | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | PICO question formulation | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | evidence-to-decision framework tables | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | a search strategy is re-runnable — databases, dates, query recorded | yes in rationale | mechanism is bibliographic | yes | fence the mechanism, keep the rationale (it is the row above) | . Three rows are platform rules; the four fenced rows are a folio’s methodology, not a backlog. Nothing is shipped for the fenced rows — empty criteria would let a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run. A folio that wants them declares them in its own repository.

640.title: What this skill does NOT do
640.content: It asserts no clinical or empirical claim, and the platform must not. The mechanism carries process — who may rule on what, given what. The evidence is the folio’s and the judgement is the guideline group’s; a platform that shipped a default answer to either would be asserting on their behalf.

Read it first; this skill adds only what evidence review instantiates. | translation-manager §”The agentic round trip” — the other instance. | voice-who-guideline-development in the IRIS replica’s style guide — how a recommendation is worded: the language of normative statements, not the process that produces them, which is this skill. | domain-fencing — the three questions, and why a fenced rule is correctly located rather than missing. | .

643.title: External registry — the role’s contract
643.content: Skill external-registry-contract: The contract the external-registry role is held to: what a trusted registry outside this layer must provide for a portal to verify what it received, and what the verifier does when it cannot. The narrowest contract the diagrams require. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: KG to public portal . external-registry in scenarios/roles.json is played by an external actor: trusted registries and observatories outside this layer’s control. A role played by something we do not run is still a role, and its skills are its contract: what we rely on it to do. A contract is not an instruction; it is what the diagrams assume.

644.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
644.content: One lane names this role: Lane_Portal in processes/kg/kg-to-portal.bpmn, holding P_Verify and GW_Verified. What that lane’s documentation, the task’s, and kg-to-portal §”Trust” require of the registry is the whole contract — nothing more is claimed.

645.title: What it must do
645.content: . | Publish the trust anchors a verifier resolves a signer’s key from — for GDHCN, a WHO SMART Trust DID trustlist (did.json), served as static JSON (PROD: tng-cdn.who.int/v2/trustlist/…). | Serve a slice by its hierarchical path, …/$domain/$participant/$usage/did.json, with - as a wildcard, so a verifier fetches only what it needs. | Nothing else. Whether a package signature can be expressed for GDHCN verifiers at all is an open question in kg-to-portal, not a promise of this role. | .

646.title: What the verifier does when the contract is not met
646.content: An unreachable registry is unknown, never a pass: GW_Verified routes it as it routes a mismatch, to the last good version (End_Rejected). This side of the contract is ours, and it is what makes relying on a party we do not control safe. Needs the owner’s review: this contract is inferred from one diagram. The test in tested-by: holds the side of it that is ours: one lane names this role, it holds P_Verify and GW_Verified, and GW_Verified serves the bytes only on a match, sending every other answer to End_Rejected. Lines 1 and 2 above are the registry’s own behaviour on a network this repository does not reach, and nothing here tests them.

648.content: Skill feature-staging: Manages feature-branch staging deployments under gh-pages/branches// for before/after publication review comparison. Handles branch creation, staging deployment, commit SHA stamping, and cleanup. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Mount a declared subgraph, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, A harness’s default rendering, Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Wireframe design review, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Is AtomicMass.lean still in sync with its data table?, Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome .

649.title: When to use this skill
649.content: When a content change is being reviewed and the reviewer (or the author) needs to see the rendered result before merging. The staging deployment puts the feature branch’s rendered site at: . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/ . A preview is the general publication step with a different root. The push itself is render-kg-to-cdn with branches/<branch-slug>/ as the publication root URL and the gh-pages Tool as the target — the same step a release takes with the site root. What this skill owns is everything around that call: the slug, the banner and staging.json, the render log, the PR comment, and taking the preview down. Which site — the repository the change lives in . <owner>/<repo> above is the repository that holds the change, not the repository of the index the agent happens to be working in. Read that repository’s index.config.json first: . | the change lives in | its preview is at | published by | . | a repository with its own site (its index.config.json has a site entry) | https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<slug>/, and the root from its default branch | that repository: stage-local.ts --repo . from its checkout when it declares site.agentRun (below), else its own staging.yml | . | a layer an index mounts and publishes as part of its own site (no site of its own) | branches/<slug>/ on the index’s site | a staging re-pin: a pull request on the index that points the mount at the branch’s commit, recorded with bun run cat mount:remote --staging (basis staging, no consent needed) | . A repository with a site of its own is previewed there, even when an index also mounts it. The index’s site shows it as one layer among its layers, which is the wrong page for that repository’s reviewers. If the repository’s own build cannot run yet (its publisher refuses for a missing cache or an undeclared input), say what is missing and ask. Never fall back to the index’s site in silence.

650.title: How it works
650.content: 1. Feature branch → staging deployment . When an agent pushes to a feature branch with an open pull request, drafts included, feature-staging.yml automatically: . | Builds the docs site (Jekyll + TypeDoc + BPMN diagrams) | Writes the build’s facts — commit SHA, timestamp, branch, PR, issue, build log — once, to staging.json at the preview root | Injects a constant staging banner at the top of every HTML page, which reads those facts in the browser | Comments on the PR that the preview is staged and queued, with the earliest push time and when it should be live | Waits for the rate-limit window (§8), then deploys to gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ only the files that differ from the live site (staging-share.ts apply). The preview’s staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live site in the browser and puts the banner back on its pages; the live site’s root 404.html (staging-share.ts write-404, written by docs-site.yml) installs that worker for a deep link opened before it exists. A page is shared only when it matches the live one once the per-preview edits are set aside (banner, SEO strip, fa-staging and fa-search-index, TypeDoc’s title suffix); anything else keeps the preview’s own copy. The footer build stamp is filled in the browser on every build, the live site’s from build.json, so an unchanged page is byte-identical across deploys | Rewrites the same comment: pushed at a time, live by about five minutes later | . 2. The staging banner . Every staged page carries a muted-sage banner: . 🔀 FEATURE BRANCH — claude/update-schedule · commit a1b2c3d · built 2026-09-18T00:30:00Z · PR #42 · issue #215 · compare with main ↗ · build log . Its colour, #4F6F52, measures 5.63:1 against its white text, above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. Check any replacement the same way; the pale decorator sages (#9CAF88, #87A96B) land near 2.5:1. The facts are fetched, not baked — and that is a storage decision . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-banner.ts injects a fragment that is byte-identical on every page and across every rebuild, and the browser derives its preview root from location.pathname, fetches staging.json and fills the banner in. A per-build value in the fragment makes every page unique on every build, so each re-push adds the whole site to gh-pages as new objects. Three rules: . | Nothing per-build may go back into the fragment. staging-banner-constant.test.ts runs two builds with different facts and compares the emitted bytes, so any leak fails regardless of how it is spelled. Add the fact to staging.json instead. | A failed fetch must still say PREVIEW. The static markup carries “FEATURE BRANCH” before any fetch happens, and the fetch only ever ADDS detail. “Could not determine” is never rendered as “this is the real site” — the same third-state rule the rest of the repository runs on, and here the failure mode is a reviewer approving the wrong artefact. | Every value from the JSON goes in as textContent, never as markup. Git ref names may contain <, > and " — they are not in git’s forbidden set, which stops at space, ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, \ and the control characters. staging-banner.e2e.ts pins this with a branch name carrying an onerror payload. | . Pages still differ between previews, because Jekyll’s relative_url prepends the baseurl to ~235 hrefs per page and the fa-translation-index island publishes site.baseurl to JavaScript. Both are coupled to the language switcher. 3. Commit SHA stamping — and the four fields staging must NOT write . Both builds write docs/_data/build.yml, and they do not write the same fields. The difference is deliberate: it is the second half of the deduplication above. |   | docs-site.yml (main) | feature-staging.yml (a preview) | . | sha, short_sha, built_at, run_url | written | DELIBERATELY ABSENT | . | branch, staging, staging_slug, pr_number, search_index | — | written | . Why staging omits them. site-chrome/_includes/footer_custom.html renders short_sha, built_at and run_url into the footer of every page, so writing them per build changes every page on every deploy. The client fills those three in from the same staging.json the banner already fetches — one request, two consumers — and a failed fetch leaves Jekyll’s | default: 'dev' in place rather than blanking the footer, which is the same third state §”The facts are fetched, not baked” requires of the banner. On main there is one copy and nothing to deduplicate, so the include’s own reason stands: “a stale browser cache and a deploy that has not run look identical.” . Adding a per-build field back to the staging stamp will not fail a test. staging-banner-constant.test.ts compares the banner fragment, which is genuinely constant; the footer is not in it, because it lives in a Jekyll include rather than in the workflow’s injection step. Check the deploy commits on gh-pages, not the code, to confirm pages do not differ across rebuilds. A Jekyll layout can read site.data.build.sha to display the deployed version — on main. Under a preview, read it from staging.json. 4. Before/after comparison . The reviewer opens both URLs side by side: . | Surface | URL | What it shows | . | Main (current) | <pages-url>/ | The published state on main | . | Staging (proposed) | <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | The feature branch’s changes | . The commit SHA on each page confirms exactly what is being compared. 5. Cleanup . When the PR is merged or closed, the cleanup job in feature-staging.yml removes branches/<slug>/ from gh-pages so stale previews don’t accumulate. The full retention rules — merged vs closed-unmerged, the label, the dispatch — are in staging-review §”Staging retention”. 6. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by size, at 3 GB in total, and the oldest are rotated off. The cap is by size rather than count because one preview can run to hundreds of megabytes. Per-PR cleanup bounds nothing in total, every preview is a full copy of the site, and a gh-pages branch past GitHub’s 10 GB Pages limit freezes the live site. So every stage run, inside its push loop, runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts: it stamps the preview it is staging (branches/<slug>/.staged-at), keeps that one plus the most recently updated others while the total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES (3 GB, 3 x 1024^3 bytes, defined there and nowhere else), and removes the rest, oldest first — each with a removed render-log entry, its record retired into branches/_retired/, and a line (slug, age, size) in the commit message and job log. _retired/ and non-preview entries are never touched. Two things to know when editing it: . | The push loop re-reads gh-pages on every attempt; it does not rebase. The commit carries removals decided against one read of the branch, and a replayed removal is a stale one — it could delete a preview another run has just refreshed. Same shape as publish-gh-pages.sh. | A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. It can reach an OPEN PR’s preview; the cost is a 404 until the author pushes, not lost work. Detail and the reviewer’s remedy: staging-review §”The cap”. | . 7. The cone — a preview rebuilds only what a changed file can reach . A preview rebuilds only the dependency cone of the changed files, at FILE level, with each derived directory’s generator declared as writer. The rule is general across rendered kinds. A rendered directory is in the cone when a changed file is . | under its own path (its pages, or its source data), or | in the import closure of a writer it declares, or under a writer directory (a path ending in /: what a generator reads, such as its templates, rather than imports), or | in a directory it is derivedFrom, transitively (check:derived-from --downstream <instance/id> prints that half on its own). | . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-cone.ts computes it; compose-docs.ts carriedInstances applies it to the composed layers. Three rules: . | Any doubt carries. No file list, a writer that does not exist, or an import that does not resolve carries the directory, with the reason in the build log. A preview missing the pages under review misleads a reviewer, while an oversized one only costs bytes. | A computed import() is bounded, not ignored. It can load only a module, so it carries on a changed module file and never on a page. The two such sites a generator reaches today (harness-config.ts’s contributes loader and block-module.ts’s block loader) have DECLARED targets and are walked exactly; DECLARED_COMPUTED_IMPORTS lists them. | The instance-prefix match is a floor. The cone can only add to it. Narrowing below it is a separate decision, made once the cone has been measured in previews. | . A skill-only change carries no IG; a change to gen-ig-pages.ts or to the DAK layer’s themes/chrome.json carries all three. staging-cone.test.ts holds these cases as tests. Built sites follow the same rule. An IG’s own Jekyll site and its AST site are BUILT in the preview from an upstream repository pinned in the layer’s own files, not composed from the checkout. stage-ig-sites.ts and stage-ast-sites.ts take --changed-files and stage only the layers siteInCone reaches. Its reasons, in order: no file list; a change to the build environment (SITE_ENVIRONMENT: the docs Gemfile and this workflow); a change under the layer; the cone reaching any of the layer’s directories (a theme change arrives this way); or a change in the stager’s closure. Each decision is printed with its reason. When you add a generated directory, declare its writer and derivedFrom. Without them the cone cannot reach it through code or data, and the prefix floor is all it gets. 8. The rate limit — a preview never cancels the main site’s Pages build . Staging previews are pushed to gh-pages at a limited rate. GitHub’s pages build and deployment keeps only the NEWEST run, so every push cancels the build in flight, the main site’s included; a build takes about three minutes. So before each push attempt the stage job re-reads gh-pages and runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-push-gate.ts gate, which holds the push until the branch tip is old enough: . | tip of gh-pages | wait until it is | . | a staging commit (staging(...)) | STAGING_WINDOW_MS — 5 min | . | anything else: the main-site publish, publish.yml, any other publisher | MAIN_WINDOW_MS — 10 min | . The numbers live once, in that script. Exit 75 means it slept until the window should open (plus up to a minute of jitter) and the loop must re-read and ask again; exit 1 means the job has waited MAX_WAIT_MS (two hours) and fails rather than pushing; exit 2 is an unreadable tip, never read as open. Three things to know when editing it: . | git’s fast-forward rule is the lock. Two jobs that both find the window open both build on the same tip; one push is rejected, re-reads, finds a tip younger than the window, and waits. So at most one staging push lands per window with no shared state. A rejection whose tip MOVED is therefore a lost race, sent back to the gate without spending one of the three attempts; only a rejection with the tip unmoved counts as a failure. | No concurrency group, and none should be added. Every waiting preview would pend in one group and each arrival would cancel the last. The per-branch group at the workflow level stays: a newer push to the same PR cancels a preview still waiting at the gate, so a superseded preview is never pushed at all. | A staging push BEFORE a main-site push is harmless; only one AFTER it cancels the build that matters. The main push then cancels the staging build, and the build that runs carries both. That is why the gate looks at the tip, and why it does not wait for docs-site runs that have not pushed yet. | . A rate limit is used rather than a batching flush job because the gate is one script and one loop whose correctness rests on git, while a flush job needs a second workflow, an artifact round trip per preview, a record of what is deployed, a best-effort schedule and a write token over content built from a pull request. The cost is latency under load: with K previews waiting, the last one pushes about 5 × K minutes later, and the PR comment gives its own estimate. The cleanup and cleanup-dispatch jobs do NOT pass through the gate. They push once per closed PR rather than once per push. 9. Build types — preview and full . There are two build types. A public comment (PC) build is a full build, and so is a release. | build type | used for | builds | . | preview | every pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview | only what the change can reach (the cone, §7); every whole-corpus index is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt | . | full | the main site deploy, a public comment release, a release | everything; every index rebuilt from the tree being published | . An index is computed over the whole corpus: the search index, the LSI viewer, the SQLite slices, the handler index, the glossary pages, the translation status pages and the node-kind pages. A builtAtPublish entry says so with index: true; a writer is borrowed only when every entry it writes says so. Rebuilding an index in a preview shows the reviewer almost nothing and costs minutes, so in a preview derive:publish puts back main’s copy from main’s writer-cone recording and logs borrowed <writer>; the search index is served from main the same way (§”Serve the published search index” in the preview workflow). So a preview of a glossary, translation or node-kind change shows main’s copy of those pages: review such a change on a full build (dispatch with build_type: full) or in its source. The switch is CAT_BUILD_TYPE (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/build-type.ts). Any doubt builds full: unset means full, and a value that is neither word is refused. A preview whose main recording holds no copy of an index builds it. A public comment release must be frozen from a full build. A frozen release is cited by page and line for the whole comment period, so its search and slices must describe the draft, not main. Dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, then run pc:release freeze. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json. 10. Agent-built previews — deferred on the critical path, verified by a full CI rebuild . When an agent builds and pushes a preview with stage-local.ts, it writes branches/<slug>/_build-record.json (scripts/preview-record.ts) recording builder: "agent", the git tree hash tree of the source tree it built (HEAD^{tree} or the merge tree with origin/main), the head and base commit SHAs, and the SHA-256 of every deployed file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When feature-staging.yml runs on the pull request: . | Defer on the critical path. conflict-gate checks branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages. When builder is "agent" and record.tree equals MERGE_SHA^{tree} (refs/pull/<n>/merge), the preview is already live for that exact merge tree: the workflow sets the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, posts a <!-- preview-build-verify --> notice on the PR, and skips the critical-path stage build so the runner is free. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) builds on the critical path as usual. | Verify off the critical path. preview-verify-sweep.yml (triggered when feature-staging.yml completes and on a 15-minute schedule) checks that no Feature Staging run is queued or in progress, finds the oldest open PR whose head commit has preview/agent-build in state pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr=<number>. | Compare or replace. The verify run rebuilds refs/pull/<n>/merge in full and runs preview-record.ts compare against the agent’s _build-record.json on gh-pages: . | Files match (same=true): nothing is redeployed; preview/agent-build is set to success (or failure if a built-site check failed) and the PR comment records the verified tree. | Files differ (same=false) or the base moved (same=stale): CI’s build is deployed to branches/<slug>/ (guarded so a newer preview tree is never overwritten) with a rendered log entry, and when the agent’s build differed, preview/agent-build is set to failure with the differing file paths listed in the PR comment. | Merge guard: merge-guard check 5 (src/coordinator/merge-guard.ts) reads preview/agent-build alongside check runs; pending holds the PR as not ready, and failure refuses the merge. | . | .

651.title: Agent workflow
651.content: When an author requests a content change: . | Detect scope — use content-graph and integration-watcher to identify affected blocks and downstream implications | Create feature branch — branch from main, open PR immediately | Make changes — edit content blocks, deterministic logic, translations | Push — on a folio whose staging.yml runs on push, the staging deployment happens automatically. On an agent-run repository, run stage-local.ts (below). | Report staging URL — tell the author the preview is at <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | Iterate — each push updates the staging deployment with a new SHA | . The BPMN for this workflow is the content core’s processes/content/content-change-review.bpmn. Publishing without a runner — stage-local.ts, one command . When the Actions queue is backed up, the agent can build and publish itself: it already has the checkout, the platform and bun. On an agent-run repository (below) this is not a shortcut. It is the only publish path. It is one command for a preview and for the main site, for a folio and for a FHIR IG: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --plan # what it would do; nothing built bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --dry-run # build, compose the commit, push nothing bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> # build and push bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --artifact <dir> . It prints its plan first, every time: which workflow it mirrors, where the output lands, what it replaces and what it keeps, the commit message, and what it does not run. The size review. Owner, 2026-11-10: “add size review as part of authoring process”. Every build, preview or main, prints a size report before its push (site-size.ts, bun run cat site:size). The report gives the total against the published root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. It writes site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. The review is advisory: growth over 10% or 10 MB is a warning, and nothing is refused. Read the report before you hand over the preview. The usual culprits each have one fix: . | another layer’s pages copied in: link that layer’s own site; | the same bytes under several names: publish one index, and serve each file once; | vendored libraries: serve them from the shared-assets host; | .map files: do not publish them. | . When the growth holds and none of these fixes applies, raise a decision card with the owner, with the comparison line and the top contributing directories on it. Which publisher is read from the repository’s own workflow files, from the reusable workflow each one calls: . | a caller of folio-staging.yml is a folio. The build inputs (build_command, site_dir, publish_branch, …) are read from that caller. | a caller of a reusable workflow that a mounted layer declares as a site publisher is that publisher’s kind. The IG layer declares one: a caller of its fhirbuild.yml or ghbuild.yml is an IG, published by that layer’s own code, which stage-local.ts reaches through the layer’s declared site-publisher-ig pipeline slot and never by path. The reusable workflow is fetched at the ref the caller names, and its build job is run step by step as written: run: blocks with the environment a runner gives them, docker:// steps in their image. Steps that read a secret, push to the source branch, or need an Actions runtime are skipped, and the plan names each one with its reason. fhirbuild.yml itself only triggers build.fhir.org’s auto-build, so the Pages build is the ghbuild.yml beside it, and the plan says so. | a repository that calls both (smart-ra carries an IG under input/) gets the folio, unless --publisher ig is given. The folio owns the publish root. An IG’s root deploy is a clean one, and it is refused on a publish branch that holds a folio’s branches/, _render-log/ or _main-site.json. | . Main site or preview follows the branch, as the workflows do. The default branch publishes the main site; any other branch publishes a preview. --main says the same explicitly, and it is refused off the default branch. The main site is published only from a HEAD that is the pushed tip of the default branch. |   | folio | IG | . | preview | branches/<slug>/, replaced wholesale; held by the rate-limit gate (§8); commit staging(<slug>): from <sha>; render log staging-preview | branches/<last path component>/, nothing deleted; commit Deploy candidate branch | . | main site | the root, through publish-main-site.ts: only the files the last publish’s _main-site.json lists are replaced, and branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are kept; commit main-site: from <sha>; render log main-site for / | the root, cleaned except for the deploy step’s clean-exclude (branches, sitepreview) and the action’s own exclusions; commit Deploy main branch | . Every path refuses an empty build before it deletes anything. | Pushing removes the first wait and not the second. Pages deploys on a runner, so say the page is live once that deploy has run, never sooner. | --artifact <dir>: no GitHub at all. It writes the same build as a bundle for a claude.ai Artifact: index.html plus the files listed in <dir>/artifact.json. Publish that, and it is live in about a minute, private until shared. | An Artifact holds at most 254 files plus the page per publish. Whole top-level directories are left out to fit, the ones with the most files first. artifact.json names each one, and links into a left-out directory 404. | Before publishing a folio whose content belongs to a real organisation (a WHO draft, say), ask the author: an Artifact is a new place that content appears. | . | What it does not do, and says in its plan: . | the folio preview’s QA sweep, screenshots, review-comment ingestion and PR comment (the banner says the preview was built locally); | the IG workflow’s PR comments, its branch-history page and README write-back (each reads a token, or writes the source branch); | the IG deploy action’s single-commit, which force-pushes one orphan commit and erases the publish branch’s history. This path commits on top and never force-pushes. | . | An IG build needs what its workflow needs. The workflow runs IG Publisher in a Docker image, so a machine with no Docker daemon gets the plan from --dry-run, and a real run stops naming the missing prerequisite. | An IG repository’s own site is built from its AST, not from the Publisher’s HTML. The repository declares site.build in its index.config.json entry (inline — never a <instance>.config.json), and that recipe’s first step restores the AST from its cache branch and refuses one that is not valid for the commit. The cache is refreshed by a Publisher run on a runner, through the IG layer’s reusable refresh workflow. It is the one workflow an agent-run IG repository dispatches, and only a person, or an agent the owner names for that run, dispatches it. The layer that owns IG builds owns the rule and the workflow; this skill names no IG step. | . Agent-run repositories — the GitHub Actions path is documented, not run . A repository is agent-run when it says so in its own index.config.json: "site": { "agentRun": true }. An agent builds and publishes its site, and its publish workflow keeps only workflow_dispatch. This skill keeps no list of them: the declaration is the list, and stage-local.ts says in every plan whether the repository declares it. For these repositories the GitHub Actions path is documentation. It says what the workflow does, so that the agent path can match it. It is not a fallback for an agent to take. | what | agent path | GitHub Actions path (documented, not run) | . | a folio preview at branches/<slug>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | folio-staging.yml job stage | . | a folio’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | folio-staging.yml job publish-main | . | an IG preview at branches/<branch>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy candidate” | . | an IG’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy main” | . | QA sweep, screenshots, review comments, PR comments | not run (the plan says so) | jobs in the workflows above | . Never dispatch the workflow, to cover a gap or for any other reason: a dispatched run contradicts the repository’s agent-run setting. When the agent path cannot do a step, say which step it is and ask. Skills that drive GitHub Actions are not to be implemented. Document what the workflows do, here and in the workflow files, so that an agent-run step can be checked against them — stage-local.ts reads the workflow files rather than restating them, so a change to a workflow’s build or layout is a change to the agent path too.

652.title: Staleness detection
652.content: The SHA stamp means staleness is always detectable: . | Staging matches PR head → the staging preview is current | Staging SHA ≠ PR head → the staging preview is stale (push again) | Main site SHA = merge commit → the publication is current | Main site SHA ≠ latest main → docs-site.yml needs to run | .

653.title: Example — a change that spans several blocks
653.content: An author needs to change the immunization schedule: . | Agent detects the change affects: . | Narrative content in the immunization chapter | Decision logic (CQL) for scheduling the next visit | Indicators that count doses administered | Referral logic for follow-up visits | . | Agent creates feature/update-immunization-schedule | Agent edits all affected blocks, assesses downstream impact | Push → staging deployment → author reviews | Author submits to the guidance review committee | Committee compares main vs branches/feature-update-immunization-schedule/ | Committee approves → merge → staging cleaned up → main site updated | .

654.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person
654.content: Check the ref, then say how long and come back. A preview push is not a served page, and the bot’s “Staging preview” comment reports at most the first, not the second — and while it says queued, not even that. List branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages before relaying the URL; quote the comment’s own push and live-by times (the rate limit in §8 can hold a push for several windows), or say the stage job takes about 22 minutes plus the wait and Pages adds 3 to 4 on top; schedule the re-check rather than promising it. The three states, and why the third is not yours to assert, are in staging-review §”Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)”. It is the same rule and it is written once, there.

655.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
655.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — cat-harness/docs/guides/x.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

656.title: Staging links
656.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.
